name: Kasner Universe with a Scalar Field
description: Kasner's anisotropic universe filled with a massless scalar field, which is also a fluid whose pressure equals its energy density. The field loosens Kasner's second condition, so all three axes can shrink together toward the singularity, and the oscillations of the vacuum come to a stop.
convention:
We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu
u} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha
u}$. The massless scalar field $\varphi$ enters through $R_{\mu
u} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_
u\varphi$ in four dimensions, and every component assumes the two conditions on the exponents of its chart.
history: The cosmic microwave radiation turned up in 1965, and by 1967 its evenness across the sky was being measured [jacobs1968]. Such measurements had "stimulated recent investigations of anisotropic cosmological models of our Universe", and Kenneth Jacobs, a predoctoral fellow at the California Institute of Technology, worked out the ones that expand at a different rate along each of three axes [jacobs1968]. He filled them with a fluid whose pressure is a fixed fraction $\gamma$ of its energy density and solved for dust, for radiation, and for $\gamma = 1$ [jacobs1968]. Yakov Zel'dovich had argued in 1961 that pressure equal to energy density is "the most rigid equation of state compatible with the requirements of relativity theory", the one whose sound travels at the speed of light, so Jacobs called his last case the "Zel'dovich universe" [zeldovich1962, jacobs1968]. Its three scale factors are powers of the time, $t^{p_1}$, $t^{p_2}$, and $t^{p_3}$, as in Kasner's vacuum [jacobs1968, kasner1921].¶Followed back toward $t = 0$, Kasner's vacuum stretches along one axis while it shrinks along the other two, because its exponents sum to one and so do their squares [kasner1921]. The stiff fluid loosens the second condition: the squares sum to $1 - q^2$, where the energy density of the fluid is $q^2c^2/16\pi Gt^2$ and $q^2$ can be anything up to $2/3$ [jacobs1968, belinskii1973]. At $q^2 = 2/3$ every exponent is $1/3$ and the universe is Friedmann's, alike in every direction [jacobs1968]. Below that, follow a ball of particles back to $t = 0$: it is drawn out into a needle as in the vacuum, or squeezed onto a line whose length stays fixed, or crushed along all three axes at once, and Jacobs listed the three as the "cigar", the "barrel", and the "point" [jacobs1968]. Once $q^2$ passes $1/2$ only the point is left [belinskii1973].¶Does the matter in a universe change how it falls into its singularity? Evgenii Lifshitz, Isaak Khalatnikov, and Vladimir Belinskii had found that a fluid with pressure a third of its energy density "results in only small corrections" to the vacuum's endless run of Kasner epochs [lifshitz1963, bkl1970, belinskii1973]. On 27 April 1972 Belinskii and Khalatnikov, at the L. D. Landau Institute of Theoretical Physics, submitted the exception: a massless scalar field $\varphi$, which gravitates as a fluid with Zel'dovich's equation of state, so that its homogeneous solution is Jacobs's metric with $\varphi \propto q\ln t$ [belinskii1973]. With all three exponents positive the curvature of space never grows fast enough to set off a bounce, and the general solution near $t = 0$ is the same metric with exponents that change from place to place [belinskii1973]. A region that starts with one negative exponent goes through "a finite number of oscillations" and comes out with three positive ones [belinskii1973]. The old argument holds only while the pressure stays below two thirds of the energy density, and for a stiff fluid the stress grows as $1/t^2$, as fast as the curvature [belinskii1973].¶Where would such a field come from? Belinskii and Khalatnikov took it from a fifth dimension: Kasner's vacuum in five dimensions, with the size of the fifth taken as a scalar field after Theodor Kaluza, is the universe with the scalar field in the four dimensions left over [belinskii1973, kaluza1921]. The five exponents obey Kasner's two conditions, so one of them is negative, while the exponents of four dimensions can all be positive [belinskii1973]. Mix the fifth dimension with the other four, which adds a vector field, and "the general solution becomes oscillatory again" [belinskii1973]. Thibault Damour, Marc Henneaux, and Hermann Nicolai wrote the same universe in the time $\tau = -\ln t$ in 2003: the logarithms of the three scale factors and the field move along a straight line at constant velocity, like a free particle [damour2003]. The space they move in is flat with one timelike direction, the field's direction is spacelike, and Kasner's two conditions say the velocity is lightlike [damour2003].¶Belinskii and Khalatnikov's general solution was the leading behaviour near $t = 0$, carrying six free functions of position, "as many as there should be" [belinskii1973]. Lars Andersson and Alan Rendall turned it into a theorem in 2001: with a scalar field or a stiff fluid, Einstein's equations have analytic solutions with no symmetry and "as many free functions as the general solution" that approach this metric point by point [andersson2001]. They called the singularities "quiescent", after the "quiescent cosmology" John Barrow had built on the stiff fluid [andersson2001]. Grigorios Fournodavlos, Igor Rodnianski, and Jared Speck proved the metric itself stable in 2023: disturb it slightly at $t = 1$, with no symmetry assumed, and the curvature still blows up along a whole spacelike surface, provided all three exponents are positive [fournodavlos2023]. The same metric describes the inside of some black holes: Alexander Frenkel, Sean Hartnoll, Jorrit Kruthoff, and Zhengyan Shi found in 2020 that a scalar field switched on at the boundary of anti-de Sitter space reaches the inside of a black hole there and "deforms the Schwarzschild singularity into a more general Kasner universe", with an exponent for the field beside the three of the metric [frenkel2020].

related.text: The universe with the field switched off. At $q = 0$ the squares of the exponents sum to one, and one axis has to stretch toward the singularity [kasner1921].
At $q^2 = 2/3$ all three exponents are $1/3$, and the metric is the flat Friedmann universe of a stiff fluid, with scale factor $t^{1/3}$ [jacobs1968].
This universe is Bianchi type I, flat space with three scale factors, filled with a stiff fluid or a massless scalar field [jacobs1968].

In vacuum the Mixmaster universe bounces from one Kasner epoch to the next without end. A massless scalar field stops the bounces after a finite number, and the universe goes on as this one does, with all three exponents positive [belinskii1973].
The same field equations, Einstein's with a massless scalar field, solved for a static sphere [janis1968].
Kasner's universe with a magnetic field in place of the scalar field. Kenneth Jacobs put the two contents together in 1969, a stiff fluid and a field along one axis [jacobs1969].

coordinates.name: Synchronous

parameters.description: Exponent along $y$, with $p_1^2 + p_2^2 + p_3^2 = 1 - q^2$
Exponent along $z$; the two conditions leave two of the four numbers free, and where $q^2 > 1/2$ all three exponents are positive

Strength of the scalar field, a pure number with $q^2 \le 2/3$: $\varphi = (qc^2/\sqrt{8\pi G})\ln t$. At $q = 0$ the metric is Kasner's vacuum, and at $q^2 = 2/3$ it is isotropic, $p_1 = p_2 = p_3 = 1/3$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ the proper time of an observer at rest, and evaluate the powers $t^{2p_i}$ with $t$ in a fixed unit of time, so they are dimensionless and the lengths sit in $x$, $y$, and $z$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Logarithmic time

parameters.description: Exponent along $y$, with $p_1^2 + p_2^2 + p_3^2 = 1 - q^2$
Exponent along $z$; the two conditions leave two of the four numbers free, and where $q^2 > 1/2$ all three exponents are positive

Strength of the scalar field, a pure number with $q^2 \le 2/3$: $\varphi = -(qc^2/\sqrt{8\pi G})\,\tau$, linear in $\tau$. At $q = 0$ the metric is Kasner's vacuum, and at $q^2 = 2/3$ it is isotropic, $p_1 = p_2 = p_3 = 1/3$
A length, $\ell = ct_0$, with $t_0$ the unit of time of the synchronous chart

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, x, y, z)$, with $\tau = -\ln(t/t_0)$ a pure number that grows without bound toward the singularity, $t$ the proper time of the synchronous chart, and $\ell = ct_0$ a length. We take components in the chart $x^0 = \tau$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Five dimensions (Kaluza-Klein)

parameters.description: Exponent along $x$ in five dimensions, with $s_1 + s_2 + s_3 + s_5 = 1$; the exponent of four dimensions along $x$ is $p_1 = (2s_1 + s_5)/(2 + s_5)$
Exponent along $y$, with $s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2 + s_5^2 = 1$; in four dimensions $p_2 = (2s_2 + s_5)/(2 + s_5)$
Exponent along $z$; in four dimensions $p_3 = (2s_3 + s_5)/(2 + s_5)$
Exponent along $w$, the extra dimension: the strength of the scalar field of four dimensions is $q = \sqrt{6}\,s_5/(2 + s_5)$, and at $s_5 = 0$ the metric is Kasner's vacuum with a flat line added

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(T, x, y, z, w)$ of five dimensions, with $w$ along the extra dimension, and evaluate the powers of $T$ with $T$ in a fixed unit of time. The metric of four dimensions is $\sqrt{g_{ww}}$ times the first four terms, with $t \propto T^{1 + s_5/2}$ its proper time and $\varphi = (c^2/\sqrt{8\pi G})\sqrt{3/2}\,s_5\ln T$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.
